True Cost

Educational use only. Not financial advice. Check the actual terms of any offer before signing.

What it does

Credit offers hide their price behind phrases like “0% EMI”, “pay in 4”, “flat 9%” or “just pay the minimum”. True Cost rewrites any offer as a list of dated cash flows and solves for the one number that makes them comparable: the annual rate you are really paying.

How it works

Every offer becomes a series of cash flows from your side of the table. At period 0 you receive the goods (worth their cash price) and pay any upfront fee; afterwards you make payments. The actuarial method finds the rate per period, \(i\), at which those flows balance:

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{CF_k}{(1+i)^{k}} = 0$$

The APR is the period rate times the number of periods in a year, \(w\) (12 for monthly, 26 for fortnightly). The effective annual yield compounds instead:

$$\text{APR} = w \cdot i \qquad\qquad \text{EAY} = (1+i)^{w} - 1$$

This is the method prescribed in the United States by Regulation Z, Appendix J. The unit tests in the repository reproduce its Example (i): $5,000 advanced, 24 monthly payments of $230, APR 9.69%.

Flat rate vs reducing balance

A flat rate charges interest on the original amount for the whole term, even though you repay part of it every month. A reducing-balance rate charges interest only on what you still owe. For a loan of \(L\) over \(n\) months at flat rate \(f\):

$$\text{payment} = \frac{L + L \cdot f \cdot n/12}{n}$$

whereas at a reducing-balance monthly rate \(r\) the payment is the ordinary annuity:

$$\text{payment} = L \cdot \frac{r(1+r)^n}{(1+r)^n - 1}$$

Since the average balance outstanding is roughly half the original, a flat rate is close to twice the reducing rate. The tool shows the exact conversion.

Why APR is the fair comparison

Total fees can mislead: a cheap-looking fee on a two-week loan can be a triple-digit annual rate, while a larger fee on a two-year loan may be modest. The APR puts every offer on the same clock. It still has limits (see below), so the tool also reports the total extra cost in currency.

Credit card minimum payments

Each month the balance grows by \(B \cdot \text{APR}/12\), then the minimum payment (the larger of a floor amount and a percentage of the balance) is subtracted. Because the minimum shrinks with the balance, the tail is very long. The simulation stops at 600 months or when the balance is cleared.

Why I built it

Limits

  • Periods are treated as equal (every month or every two weeks). Odd first periods, which Regulation Z handles with day counts, are not modelled.
  • Late fees are applied as a single missed payment that is paid one period later. Real penalty interest, collection fees or credit-score effects are not included.
  • Currency is only a label. No exchange rates are involved.
  • Credit card interest is charged on the opening monthly balance, not on daily balances, so the result is an approximation.
